analysis.investment_thesis: Inox Green fails every core Fisher criterion: revenue has shrunk at -6.1% CAGR over 7 years, net profit is declining (INR 28 Cr → 22 Cr), and ROE is a negligible 1.02%. Paying 81x P/E and 129x EV/EBITDA for a captive O&M subsidiary with no discernible innovation moat is a value destruction trap, not a growth opportunity.
key_strengths: Dramatic debt reduction — borrowings fell from INR 1,411 Cr (2021) to INR 95 Cr (2025), D/E now a clean 0.05
Wind energy sector has long-term structural tailwinds in India's renewable push
Operating margin of 14.7% is reasonable for an asset-light O&M services model
key_risks: Revenue is structurally stagnant — 7Y CAGR of -6.1% with no sign of acceleration toward Fisher's 20%+ threshold
Captive subsidiary of Inox Wind limits pricing power, customer diversity, and independent strategic vision
FY25 investing outflow of INR 637 Cr funded by INR 572 Cr equity raise signals dilutive expansion with unproven returns
red_flags: Net profit declining year-over-year: INR 28 Cr (FY24) → INR 22 Cr (FY25) despite revenue inching up to 236 Cr
ROE of 1.02% on INR 2,020 Cr equity base — capital is being destroyed, not compounded
Other income (INR 57 Cr) now exceeds operating income (INR 52 Cr), meaning the core O&M business is barely profitable on its own
OCF positive only 3 of last 5 years; free cash flow was negative in 3 of last 5 years
EV/EBITDA of 129x is unjustifiable given contracting EBITDA trend
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Through my scuttlebutt lens, this business raises immediate concerns. Inox Green is structurally a captive O&M services arm of Inox Wind — it cannot independently develop new customers, expand TAM, or pivot its product mix. Revenue has gone nowhere in seven years (INR 368 Cr in 2018, INR 236 Cr in 2025), and the recent FY23-25 average of ~INR 237 Cr shows a business in stasis, not growth. The O&M model is inherently low-innovation: there is no meaningful R&D, no product pipeline, and no evidence of management building durable competitive advantages beyond its parent relationship. For Fisher, this alone disqualifies the investment.

The valuation is the final insult to any growth investor. At P/E 81.6x and EV/EBITDA 129x, the market is pricing in a transformation that the financials simply do not support — ROE of 1%, declining net profit, and contracting EBITDA. The FY25 large investing outflow (INR 637 Cr) funded by equity dilution (INR 572 Cr in financing CF) suggests management is betting on capacity expansion, but until revenue growth, margin expansion, and double-digit ROE materialize, this stock demands an enormous leap of faith at a punishing price. I would not own this at any reasonable margin of safety.
